description: Our team brings together experience in large-scale system monitoring, AI agents, and web development and Machine Learning. Professionally, we build tools that filter noise from millions of events to surface the few that matter. For this challenge, we’re applying the same thinking to NASA’s SPHEREx data: making changes in the sky between observations easy for anyone to see, explore, and share.
summary: Nakshatra is the SPHEREx Sky Change Viewer: a free website that turns NASA's 89 TB all-sky infrared archive into something anyone can look at. Type an object's name or a place and it fetches only the cutouts needed from NASA/IPAC IRSA, removes the zodiacal dust glow, puts every photo on one scale and flips through them in time order, with the object's JPL Horizons position ringed. Its key innovation is that it does not stop at a prediction. In each photo it measures whether SPHEREx actually recorded the object and answers detected, marginal or predicted only, and beside every non-detection it states the faintest source that photo could show, a number we validated against injected test sources to 0.01 magnitude. Every claim carries an evidence label (observed, derived, interpreted or unverified), and any AI-written text is checked against that evidence. Result: Makemake is present at S/N 10.8 and 10.3, then gone a year later because it moved, not because it faded. For Planet X, it shows what a single photo can and cannot reveal. Free, no login, shareable by link.
details:
NAKSHATRA: THE SPHEREX SKY CHANGE VIEWER

See what moved. Know how sure we are.

A free website that turns NASA's 89 TB all-sky infrared archive into photos anyone can flip through, then measures whether the telescope really recorded what you are looking for. No login, and the link carries the exact view.

1. THE PROBLEM

SPHEREx re-photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours. A distant moving world, such as a dwarf planet beyond Neptune or a hypothetical Planet X, leaves a trace in those photos, but nobody can easily see it:

  • 89 TB of photographs to look through
  • About 75% of a raw frame's signal is zodiacal dust light, so a raw photo is a flat grey wash
  • Every photo is a different colour and date

The usual result is a prediction ("it should be here") that nobody checks against the pixels.

SPHEREx all-sky infrared map. Source: NASA SPHEREx, via IPAC.

2. WHAT IT DOES

Four things, in the order a visitor meets them:

  • Look. Type an object (Makemake, Ceres) or coordinates. The server fetches only the needed cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, subtracts the zodiacal light, puts every photo north-up on one brightness scale and plays them in time order, with the object's JPL Horizons position ringed.
  • Measure. One click tests whether SPHEREx actually recorded it and says detected, marginal or predicted only.
  • Investigate. Pin photos, measurements and claims into a case. An evidence board shows what holds together. Export a report (HTML, Markdown, JSON).
  • Learn. Learner mode explains each term and offers mysteries to solve with real photos. Explorer and Investigator modes reveal more controls and numbers.

The five Space Apps challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis) all open with their photo series. Here is the viewer following the asteroid Felicia:

Photos in time order, the object's path across the sky and its place in the Solar System, on one screen.

3. HOW IT WORKS: KEY INNOVATIONS

Every answer goes through the same six steps:

From a typed name to a measured, labelled answer.

Architecture. The viewer is a thin layer. The browser talks to one Flask service, which fetches only the cutouts it needs from NASA/IPAC IRSA, positions and orbits from JPL, names from NED and stars from Gaia, measures them, and keeps a shared sky index, a cache and saved cases in Postgres. The optional writing agents sit beside it and can never change a measurement.

Architecture: browser, one small service, free public archives, and a database.

  • Measure, don't just ring. In each photo we place a 3x3-pixel aperture at the predicted position and compute signal-to-noise against noise calibrated on real empty sky.
  • "Predicted only" never means "absent". Beside every non-detection we show the faintest source that photo could have shown. We checked that limit against sources we injected into 25 real cutouts: it agrees to 0.01 magnitude.
  • Four evidence states on every claim: observed, derived, interpreted, unverified. A conclusion is never stronger than the weakest pin beneath it, and the app says so.
  • A change fingerprint that separates a lasting change from a flash, a flicker or a wanderer, and never mistakes a steady star seen at different colours for a change (0% false calls on constant stars in simulation).
  • A model may write, never decide. Optional language-model agents draft summaries; every sentence is checked against the pinned evidence, ungrounded paragraphs are dropped, and a plain template takes over when no model is available.
  • Built lean. A shared sky index of about 1.6 million frames in Postgres, and a 62 MB peak for a 47-photo measurement, so it runs on a 512 MB free server.

The measurement is only as good as its noise estimate, so we tested ours on real empty sky. Our own validation found the first version overstated the signal-to-noise and we fixed it:

Spread of S/N on empty sky: 1.6 to 2.8 before the fix, 1.04 after (1.0 is perfect).

4. RESULTS: CASE STUDIES AND VALIDATION

Makemake: here, then gone

Makemake is a dwarf planet about 52.7 AU from the Sun. SPHEREx photographed its predicted position 62 times in 12 visits. In the first pass the signal-to-noise at that spot is 10.8 and 10.3. A year later the same spot reads -0.2 and -0.3. The object did not fade, it moved:

S/N at Makemake's predicted position. Above 5 sigma means clearly seen.

This is what the viewer shows: the first pass with the object ringed, and the same spot a year later, empty.

"Here, then gone": the same patch of sky, a year apart.

Is the ring really on the object?

For three known objects we compared the signal at the JPL-predicted position with six control positions in the same photos. Near V 17 the ring is clearly above the controls, and recall falls as the object fades. Not detected at V 17 or fainter means below one photo's depth, not absent.

Share of 14 photos at 5 sigma or more, at the ring and at six control positions.

How faint can one photo see?

We injected point sources of known brightness into empty positions of 60 real cutouts. Half are recovered near AB magnitude 16.0 in a single photo. The depth limit shown beside every "predicted only" comes from each photo's own noise, and matches this experiment to -0.01 magnitude (scatter 0.05).

Recovery of injected sources against brightness.

False alarms

Noise alone is symmetric, so its negative tail is the false-positive rate. Across 33,768 random positions in 120 real cutouts, only 0.16% read 5 sigma or more below the background by chance:

From the product walkthrough: what counts as "seen".

The scoreboard

Every figure on this page comes from our published validation report: 0.16% false alarms, noise spread 1.04, depth near AB 16, ring against controls 79% / 12% for Felicia, and 525 automated tests passing. Two earlier claims we could not support were retired in public.

What we can actually back up.

5. BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  • Researchers get a fast first look and a measured detection check before heavy pipeline work, plus a citable report with sources and DOIs.
  • Learners and the public can watch a dwarf planet move across real SPHEREx photos and understand why one photo cannot prove it is absent.
  • For Planet X, it gives an honest picture of what SPHEREx can and cannot see at these depths, which is where any search for a distant world has to start.

Learner mode turns this into a game: plant a fake Planet X into real photographs, then find the edge of the telescope's sight.

"Plant your own Planet X": a learner exercise on real photographs.

6. COST, BUSINESS MODEL AND SUSTAINABILITY

Nakshatra is a public-good tool, not a start-up: no login, no ads, no tracking, nothing is sold. This section shows what it costs to run, why that cost stays near zero, and how it stays alive.

What it costs today

  • Web hosting: one web service on Render's free plan. Cost: $0.
  • Database: a Supabase Postgres database holding a shared sky index of about 1.6 million frames, on a free tier. Cost: $0.
  • Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA, JPL, NED and ESA Gaia are free public archives. Cost: $0.
  • Writing agent: optional, on Groq's free tier, with a template fallback if it is unavailable. Cost: $0.
  • People: volunteer hackathon time, with no salaries and no paid services.

Infrastructure spend so far: $0 a month. The picture below shows today's costs next to what a busier deployment would plausibly cost.

Running cost today against a busier deployment. The right-hand figures are indicative list prices, not measured bills.

Why the cost stays low

  • No mirror of the archive. We fetch only the small cutouts a visitor asks for, never the 89 TB.
  • Cache first. A cold photo takes 5 to 20 seconds (one archive download); a cached one is instant, so cost per view falls as usage grows.
  • Small footprint. One worker, at most two concurrent renders, and a 62 MB peak for a 47-photo measurement, so a 512 MB free server is enough.
  • No accounts. No login, no user database to secure or pay for. A case is a link plus a secret edit token.

If usage grows (a plan, not a result)

Classroom-scale traffic would move hosting and the database to small paid tiers, roughly $7 and $25 a month at current list prices, plus a few dollars of pay-per-use for the optional writing agent: about $30 to $50 a month in total. The code is unchanged: the same service runs on a larger instance.

R&D cost

500 hours of team effort, valued at $40 an hour, is a notional $20,000. No cash was spent: it is volunteer time. The output is about 22,000 lines of code, 525 automated tests, 67 commits and a published validation report. Validation and tests took a quarter of the effort, because the measurements are the product.

Where the R&D effort went. The split between workstreams is our estimate; the totals are the team's recorded effort.

Business integration model

Nakshatra sits between free public archives and the people who want to use them. Data comes in from NASA and partner services; answers go out as links, reports and public endpoints, so a partner can adopt it without a contract or an integration project.

Partners on the left, users on the right, and the four integration points already built.

Pricing model (proposal)

The core is free forever. Pricing exists only where an institution needs more than the public service offers. It is set cost-plus from our hosting bill and has not yet been tested with customers. The notional R&D of $20,000 equals about 34 institution-years at $49 a month, which is why this stays a public good funded by grants and sponsors, not a profit business.

Three tiers, and the arithmetic that sets them.

Business model: how it stays alive

This is a public good, so the model is free for everyone, with funding paths for the small hosting bill. None of these is secured today.

  • Institutional hosting and embedding. Archives, universities, schools and planetariums can host their own copy or link to a view, because the link carries the exact view.
  • Small grants and sponsorship to cover hosting as traffic grows.
  • Education partnerships. Learner mode and the mysteries are classroom-ready, and teachers need nothing installed.
  • Open code. Anyone can run or extend it, so the project does not depend on one host.

Risks and how we handle them

  • Upstream change. IRSA recently dropped one release from its search service; we kept a bundled copy of that release's index so those photos still load.
  • Free-tier limits. Cold starts and rate limits are handled with caching, a wait-and-retry on the writing agent, and a plain template fallback.
  • Over-claiming. Every claim carries an evidence label, and claims we could not support were retired in public.

How we will know it works (targets, not results)

500+ users, 30% of visitors finishing a mystery, and 100+ shared links in three months. These are goals; we report no usage numbers yet.

7. ROADMAP

  • Stack several photos to go below the single-photo depth (AB 16.6).
  • Images inside exported reports, so a case can be handed over as a single document.
  • Enrichment from new object catalogues, including interstellar visitors.
  • Accessibility audit: colour contrast and screen-reader use are not yet measured.

8. HONEST LIMITS

  • We do not claim to have found Planet X.
  • Fainter than about AB 16.6 in a single photo is below depth.
  • A cold photo takes 5 to 20 seconds (one archive download); cached photos are instant.
  • User-count and share-link goals are targets, not results.

9. TOOLS AND DATA

Python, Flask, astropy and numpy; React and Vite; Supabase Postgres; hosted on Render. Data from NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx), JPL Horizons and Small-Body Database, NED, ESA Gaia, the Minor Planet Center, Legacy Surveys and Pan-STARRS. Optional writing agents: Groq (gpt-oss-120b) or Ollama. Code: https://github.com/CoderRayMan/nasa_spherex_nakshtra

10. USE OF AI

We used an AI coding assistant (Claude) to help write and test code and to draft and edit this text. Optional language-model agents (Groq, Ollama) inside the app draft case summaries only. Every sentence is checked against the pinned evidence, and the app falls back to a template without a model. No AI chooses or changes a measurement. All pictures here are screenshots of our own app, charts drawn from our validation numbers, or NASA SPHEREx imagery; none is AI-generated imagery. The charts and the demo deck were produced by code written with Claude, from our own measured numbers.
